analysis.one_liner: Extends foreclosure and eviction protections for servicemembers and raises penalties for mortgage abuses.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in two House subcommittees for the rest of the 112th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would double, from nine months to two years, the window after military service during which a servicemember's home cannot be sold, foreclosed, or seized, and would make those protections permanent instead of expiring. It would also upgrade unlawful evictions and unlawful foreclosures of servicemembers' homes from misdemeanors to felonies with up to two years in prison, and roughly double the civil fines. It was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees, where it remained without action until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Servicemembers and veterans with mortgages, and their families, who would have two years rather than nine months after military service before their home could be foreclosed or seized, plus stronger criminal and civil penalties against anyone who evicts or forecloses on them unlawfully.

how_it_helps.text: Extends from 9 months to 24 months after military service the period protecting a servicemember's home from sale, foreclosure, or seizure, and the stay of related court proceedings [S2] [S3].
Repeals the expiration date for these foreclosure protections that Congress set in the Housing and Economic Recovery Act of 2008, making them permanent [S2] [S3].

Upgrades unlawful eviction or distress of a servicemember, and unlawful sale, foreclosure, or seizure of their property, from misdemeanors to felonies with prison terms raised from one year to two years [S2] [S3].
Roughly doubles the civil penalties for these mortgage abuses, from $55,000 to $110,000 and from $110,000 to $220,000 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders and servicers, who would face a longer period during which they cannot foreclose on homes of former servicemembers, larger fines, and felony exposure for wrongful evictions and foreclosures. Some of that cost could be passed to future borrowers through pricing.

drawbacks.text: Extending foreclosure protections to 24 months after military service goes well beyond the period of actual service; lenders argue the existing nine-month window already balances protection with the practicalities of lending, and longer restrictions can raise costs or risk premiums on loans to military borrowers [S3].

Doubling criminal and civil penalties applies to lenders and servicers in cases where facts are disputed, and the bill directs the Sentencing Commission to rewrite guidelines accordingly, which increases compliance and legal costs across mortgage servicing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For servicemembers and their families, the added protection is substantial and targeted at a group Congress has long treated as needing special safeguards against foreclosure while deployed. The costs fall on lenders and servicers and only partly reach consumers through loan pricing; the main design question is whether two years after service is more protection than the problem warrants. On balance the bill's benefits to a vulnerable group outweigh its costs.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Veterans' Affairs and Judiciary committees and then to subcommittees, and neither panel ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Walz introduced the bill on April 14, 2011, with Reps. Michaud and Kissell as original cosponsors, and it drew one additional cosponsor (2 total) [S1] [S4] [S5].
The House referred it to the Veterans' Affairs Committee and the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction [S5].

In late April and August 2011 it was referred to the Economic Opportunity subcommittee and the Courts, Commercial and Administrative Law subcommittee; no hearings, markups, or floor votes followed [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders and servicers came out ahead: they kept the existing nine-month foreclosure window and the lower misdemeanor-and-fine penalty structure, because no committee ever advanced the bill. Servicemembers gained nothing beyond the protections already in law.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Democrats, and no member or group is on record opposing it.

industries.note: The bill would have doubled the post-service foreclosure prohibition window and roughly doubled civil fines while making wrongful evictions and foreclosures of servicemembers' homes felonies. Its interest ran against the servicemembers the bill protected, since the industry's gain under the status quo is the ability to foreclose sooner with smaller penalties.

Felony exposure and doubled civil penalties would have raised the stakes of handling servicemember foreclosures, while the longer 24-month window could have generated more contested proceedings. The bill never advanced, so neither effect occurred.
